newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan expected to ease rules on bank shareholdings.
newsitem.headline: Japan expected to ease rules on bank shareholdings.

text.p: Japan is expected to set loose rules on shareholding by financial holding companies, something analysts say will help revitalise the financial sector but may also lead to greater control by banks of Japanese industry.

Draft guidelines covering the lifting of a decades-old ban on holding firms unveiled last month place no restriction on shareholding by financial holding firms as long as free-and-fair competition is not inhibited. The guidelines are due to be finalised by Japan's anti-monopoly watchdog, the Fair Trade Commission (FTC), in December.
At present, big Japanese banks are banned from owning more than five percent of the shares of other companies, while insurers are prohibited from owning more than 10 percent.

Financial holding companies are expected to act as a catalyst to revitalise Japan's long-regulated financial industry and to promote the nation's "Big Bang" reforms aimed at breaking down barriers between banks, brokers and insurers.
Masaaki Higashida, a strategist at Nomura Securities Co Ltd, said, however, that an increase in banks' shareholdings could enhance their control over industries and be negative for the stock market.

"If Japanese banks are allowed to own more shares (through holding companies), it would counter the move to cut assets held by banks. It is not desirable when taking into account the type of shareholders in the (stock) market in the medium- to long-term future," Higashida said.
Japan is rare among industrialised countries in allowing banks to hold shares, and the securities industry has criticised the system as enabling banks to wield power over non-financial sectors.
Banks hold a large amount of shares in firms, in a web of interconnected stockholdings to maintain close business ties and support overall stock prices.

According to a survey by by the National Conference of Stock Exchanges, Japan's long-term credit banks, commercial banks and regional banks owned 15.1 percent of the shares of listed Japanese companies as of the end of March, 1997. The figure jumps to 41.3 percent when all financial insitutions, such as insurers and trust banks, are included.
In June, parliament revised Japan's anti-monopoly law to lift a ban on holding companies that was imposed by U.S. occupation forces after World War Two. The revision will take effect by mid-December.
Holding firms control one or more other firms, often by holding a majority stake in them, but do not themselves engage in a specific business.
The Ministry of Finance (MOF) is working out a separate bill allowing for the establishment of financial holding firms.
A ministry official said that MOF intends to submit the bill to an extraordinary session of parliament this autumn. He said, however, that details have not yet been decided.
An official at the powerful business lobby Keidanren said the Finance Ministry would decide details of shareholdings by financial holding firms.
"Restrictions on shareholdings by a financial holding firm are necessary and it is MOF which will determine them," he said.
He said MOF might set an upper limit on shareholdings at 10 percent, the same as that for insurers.
He also said that to implement the system of financial holding firms smoothly and to avoid jeopardising the stock market, MOF may set a transition period.
